title: The death of John the Baptist (29 August)
hook: the prophet dies for telling a king the truth

segments.voice: Yesterday, Joseph Calasanz, who taught children whose families couldn't pay. Your line was free schools. Did you give something to a school that doesn't charge? Day one thousand twenty.

The party is already loud. It's King Herod's birthday, and around his table sit his lords, his officers, the leading men of Galilee. Somewhere under his power sits a prisoner: a man who once wore camel hair by the Jordan, whom the king has locked up but can't quite bring himself to kill. Then a girl comes in and dances, and the king is so pleased that he makes a promise out loud, in front of everyone. Ask me for whatever you want, up to half my kingdom. She goes out to ask her mother what she should ask for. Today, a feast that keeps a death: the prophet who told a king the truth.
screen: `A KING'S BIRTHDAY.` → `A PRISONER HE WON'T KILL.` → `A PROMISE IN FRONT OF EVERYONE.`

segments.voice: Mark tells it in his sixth chapter. Herod had married Herodias, his brother's wife. And John had said to him, in the Douay-Rheims: "It is not lawful for thee to have thy brother's wife." That's the whole offense. One sentence, and true. Herodias wanted him dead. Herod didn't, not quite. Mark gives a strange, honest detail: Herod feared John, "knowing him to be a just and holy man," and he liked to listen to him. So the king kept the prophet locked up, and kept coming back to hear him. Then the dance, and the promise. The girl's mother tells her what to ask for: the head of John the Baptist. The girl hurries back and adds: on a dish. Here is the moment the story turns on. Mark says the king was struck with sorrow. But he had sworn, and his guests were watching. He couldn't stand to back down at his own party. So he sent the executioner. Afterward, John's disciples came, took his body, and laid it in a tomb. Notice who is free in this story and who isn't. The king has the throne, the guests and the power, and he's trapped by an oath he made to look generous. The prisoner has nothing, and he's the one person in the room who said what was true. The Church calls this day the passion of John the Baptist, the same word it uses for the suffering of Christ. All his life John went ahead of Jesus, preparing the way. Catholics see him going ahead of Jesus here, too.
screen: `IT IS NOT LAWFUL FOR THEE.` · `HEROD FEARED HIM, AND LISTENED.` · `TRAPPED BY HIS OWN OATH.` · `GOING AHEAD, EVEN IN DEATH.` · then, large: `A JUST AND HOLY MAN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: Herod's seat, and John's place. Settle, and breathe. First, Herod's seat. Is there something you keep up only because people are watching? A position, a promise, a story about yourself. Just notice it. Then John's place. Is there a truth someone close to you needs, and you've been sparing yourself the cost of saying it? Don't write the speech. Bring the person to mind, and ask what they would need to know first: that you're on their side. If you pray, you can ask Saint John the Baptist for his courage. If you don't, just hold that person with goodwill. The bell holds the time.
Passion, the Church's word for John the Baptist's death: the prophet killed for telling King Herod the truth, kept on the twenty-ninth of August.
Your line: truth cost his head. Today, tell one hard truth, kindly, to someone who needs to hear it, and choose your words before you say them. Day one thousand twenty.

howItsDone: On 29 August Catholics keep the Passion of Saint John the Baptist; the Gospel at Mass that day tells his death from the sixth chapter of Mark.

fork.setup: you're Herod. the girl asks for the prophet's head. you're sorry, but you swore in front of all your guests. what do you do?
options: keep the oath, and send the executioner.
break the oath, and let the room watch you back down.
stall, and hope she changes her mind.
fork.reveal: he kept the oath to save face. in the story, the king is the one who isn't free.

original.note: Greek: it is permitted, it is lawful. in Mark 6:18 John tells the king it is not: οὐκ ἔξεστιν.

trapdoor: what you thought: a gruesome story about a head on a dish.
what it means: a prophet killed for one true sentence, and a king trapped by his own oath and his guests' eyes.
what a scholar hears: the Church calls the day John's passion, the word used for Christ's suffering; the one who went ahead of Jesus goes ahead in death too.

notes: The name Salome (from Josephus) is left out; Mark's manuscripts differ on how the girl is named (some read 'his daughter Herodias' at 6:22), so the script says only 'a girl'.
'Somewhere under his power sits a prisoner': Mark does not say where John was held (Josephus says Machaerus); kept vague on purpose.
'The Church calls this day the passion of John the Baptist': the Latin title is Passio S. Ioannis Baptistae. Confirm the English usage.
'Catholics see him going ahead of Jesus here, too': the forerunner-in-death theme is in the liturgy (e.g. Bede's homily read in the Office). Confirm phrasing.
Original: ἔξεστιν, Mark 6:18 οὐκ ἔξεστίν σοι. Confirm.
Confirm Douay-Rheims wording of Mark 6:18 and 6:20.
